currentContext.strengths: Part of the JK Organisation, a diversified industrial group with a 140+ year legacy, lending brand trust and institutional depth|Renewable power meets ~47% of total electrical consumption, among the best ratios in the industry, supporting cost and ESG positioning|Nationally distributed operational footprint (3 integrated plants + 4 grinding units across 20 states) enabling efficient market access and logistics optimisation|June 2025 merger with Udaipur Cement Works Ltd. strengthened scale, synergies, and financial resilience|Digitalisation push (AI/ML/IoT, RPA, AI-based Advanced Process Control at Udaipur) improving efficiency and cost control|Long-term credit rating of AA (Stable) from CRISIL and CARE, and highest short-term rating A1+ from both, supporting access to capital|Limestone mine acquisition in Assam underpins long-term strategic commitment to the high-growth Eastern market|Low-carbon product innovation (Green PRO LC3) launched at Sirohi, differentiating on sustainability
currentContext.strategies: Three strategic priorities for FY2025-26 and beyond: capacity expansion, cost leadership, and sustainability.|Capacity expansion programme toward 30 million tonnes by 2030, via a phased roadmap of greenfield and brownfield investments.|Efficiency enhancement programme delivering cost savings across plant operations, logistics, discount rationalisation, and geo-mix optimisation to provide structural cost insulation.|Prioritising profitable volume growth, advancing Smart Building Solutions (SBS) and premium product portfolio, deepening ESG leadership, and reinforcing presence in high-potential regional markets.|Digitalising Growth strategic direction: deploying AI, Machine Learning and IoT across sales, logistics and manufacturing to improve demand forecasting, supply-chain visibility, process optimisation and product quality (e.g., AI-based Advanced Process Control at Udaipur Raw Mill).|Brand rejuvenation ('Soch Karo Buland' / 'Aapki Chhatt Hi Aapki Neev Hai') to strengthen competitive positioning with homebuilders.|Continuous focus on de-leveraging and efficient debt management alongside judicious deployment of treasury corpus in tax-efficient instruments.|People strategy centred on employee engagement, digitalisation of HR processes (Darwin Box), and an ambition to be recognised as an Employer of Choice.|Multipronged decarbonisation strategy: Net Zero commitment, shift to renewable energy, improved energy efficiency, substitution of fossil energy with alternative fuel and raw material (AFR), low-carbon blended cement (including PPC and LC3), large-scale plantation as a carbon sink, and adoption of GHG-reducing technology.|Green+ philosophy integrating environmental responsibility across fuels, energy use and product innovation.|Strategic commitment to the high-growth Eastern market, underpinned by the limestone mine acquisition in Assam.|Dividend payout is stated to be in accordance with the Company's Board-approved Dividend Distribution Policy, one of its listed Key Policies; no further detail on payout ratio, buyback intent, or reinvestment philosophy is disclosed in this bundle beyond adherence to that policy.
currentContext.expansion: During FY2025-26, JKLC commissioned an additional Grinding Unit of 1.35 million tonnes at Surat and completed de-bottlenecking of its Cement Mill at Sirohi, taking total Company cement capacity to 18 MnMT. In June 2025, JK Lakshmi Cement Ltd. and Udaipur Cement Works Ltd. completed a landmark merger, strengthening scale, synergies and sustainability commitment, expanding geographic presence and reinforcing financial resilience. Renewable capacity additions during the year included a 9 MW solar plant at Phalodi, a 2.75 MW Floating Solar Power Plant at the Udaipur Integrated Unit, and a 7 MW solar plant at JKLC, taking total Solar Power Capacity to 124 MW from 112.10 MW. On the Smart Building Solutions (SBS) front, 5 new RMC plants were commissioned across Bhopal, Faridabad, Bhavnagar, Indore, and Durg; Tile Adhesive production was launched; and two additional Gypsum Plaster trading units were added in Rajasthan. The Company's limestone mine acquisition in Assam continues to underpin its long-term strategic commitment to the high-growth Eastern market. Separately, several projects are in the environmental-clearance pipeline per FY2025-26 EIA disclosures: expansion of limestone production capacity at the Durg (Chhattisgarh) Mine Lease II from 0.3 to 1.35 Million TPA; expansion of the captive limestone mines at Mine Lease I (Durg) from 4.8 to 8 Million TPA; a proposed standalone Cement Grinding Project of 3.0 Million TPA at Lohat, Madhubani (Bihar) for OPC/PSC/PPC/Composite Cement; and a proposed new limestone mine 'Mudhvay Sub Block A' with 2.5 Million TPA capacity at Kachchh, Gujarat. An Integrated Cement Plant proposal (Clinker 0.95 Million TPA, Cement 0.95 Million TPA producing OPC/PPC/PSC/Composite Cement) is also referenced in the EIA disclosures, though the source text is truncated before further project detail.
currentContext.mdna: Indian cement demand grew ~7% in FY2025-26, driven by government-led infrastructure programmes (PM Gati Shakti, Bharatmala, Smart Cities Mission, PMAY) and rising urbanisation/housing demand in rural and semi-urban markets.|Industry volumes are projected to expand at 6-7% per annum in the medium term, and demand is projected to grow 6-7% in FY2026-27, driven by housing and infrastructure, roads, railways, affordable housing, and Tier-II city development.|Cement price realisations remained under pressure throughout FY2025-26 due to regional competitive dynamics and continued capacity additions, and are expected to stay range-bound near term.|The West Asia conflict in Q4 FY2025-26 introduced a fresh cost headwind — pet coke, LNG, diesel and freight costs, plus rupee depreciation — compressing industry and Company margins with limited ability to pass through costs in a competitive pricing environment.|Ongoing consolidation among top industry players is expected to support pricing discipline over time, though industry capacity utilisation is projected to stay around ~70% even on an expanded base in FY2026-27.|Domestic coal substitution (reducing Hormuz-linked import exposure) is viewed as a lever that, if sustained, structurally improves cost stability.|The shared industry cost shock is seen as providing a rare justification for cement price hikes being passed on to consumers.|Company outperformed the industry (10% volume growth vs ~7% industry growth) on the strength of market presence, distribution network depth, and customer trust; total capacity reached 18 million tonnes with the Surat Grinding Unit addition.|Regional demand variation: Central and Northern regions led volume growth, Western and Eastern markets followed closely, while the South saw minimal volume growth.|Management is prioritising profitable volume growth, Smart Building Solutions and premium products, and deeper regional market presence to navigate range-bound pricing and cost headwinds into FY2026-27.

risks.risk: Margin sustainability — cost inflation outpacing price realisation
risks.note: The Company flags this as the 'central risk': input costs (especially fuel and packaging) are expected to keep rising in FY2026-27, mirroring the FY2022-23 scenario where cost increases outpaced price hikes; estimated cost rise of ₹300-400/tonne for FY2026-27 with price hikes likely to lag, widening the gap between cost inflation and realisation growth.

Industry capacity utilisation is projected to stay around ~70% even on an expanded base in FY2026-27; over 60 million MTPA of capacity was added industry-wide in FY2025-26 alone, with North India capacity growing at a 12% CAGR through FY2027-28, heightening regional price volatility and keeping sector pricing CAGR estimated in negative territory (1-2%) since FY2022-23.

risks.risk: Hormuz Strait closure — structural fuel/logistics chokepoint
risks.note: The Strait of Hormuz carries ~20% of global oil/LNG trade; Indian cement makers source ~50% of pet coke from Saudi Arabia and the UAE. Even a negotiated reopening offers limited relief, as war-risk insurance premiums (previously ~0.25% of hull value) could rise materially, keeping freight and insurance costs structurally elevated for years.

Imported petcoke and coal prices have risen ~40% and ~35% respectively since the West Asia conflict began, to an estimated $160-170/MT; with fuel and power at 30-35% of production costs, this translates to roughly ₹300/MT of unbudgeted cost pressure, and refiners shifting toward gas production could further constrain pet coke availability — a supply issue, not just a pricing one.

Shipping lines have imposed war-risk surcharges of $1,500-2,000 per container on Gulf cargo, rerouting via the Cape of Good Hope adds 10-14 days per voyage, and the Rupee's breach of 95/USD amplifies every dollar-denominated import (pet coke, gypsum, freight), compounding cost pressure from both commodity and currency risk simultaneously.

The cost of polypropylene bags used for cement packaging has nearly doubled, adding an estimated ₹60-80 per tonne, compounded by the Middle East conflict; the full effect is expected to hit margins from Q1 FY2026-27 onward, coinciding with peak fuel costs.

risks.risk: Government capex slippage and infrastructure-demand execution risk
risks.note: Infrastructure-led demand is the industry's core demand thesis, but execution risk is real: government capex declined 24% year-on-year in January 2026, and PMAY-Rural/PMGSY targets were missed in both FY2024-25 and FY2025-26; continued macro stress (conflict, inflation, fiscal compression, RBI policy constraints) could further erode the demand cushion via capex deferral and softness in private housing.

one-line thesis: JK Lakshmi navigates a severe Q4 cost shock (petcoke +40% QoQ) with limited pricing power, compressing EBITDA/ton to ~INR730, while aggressively pursuing a INR5,500+ crore capex plan to reach 30MT by 2030 despite the derecognition of INR325 crore intangible assets from the cancelled Assam mining contract.

growth verticals / optionality: 30MT capacity target by 2030 (from ~18MT now); Durg expansion (East), Northeast greenfield (Assam based on 2 auctioned mines, 250MT reserves), Kutch (FY30), Nagaur (delayed due to Aravalli SC ruling).
margins & cost dynamics: Fuel cost surge: Petcoke +40% QoQ (~$160/ton), Coal +30% QoQ; Guided cost increase INR300/ton (energy) + INR80-100/ton (packaging); Mitigation via fuel mix change in North, renewable energy (46% mix), AI/ML in pyro/grinding.
capex / expansion: Total ~INR5,500-6,000cr over FY27-FY29; INR500cr spent on Durg by FY26 end; Railway siding delays (PWD/SAIL dependencies) but ops unaffected.
capital allocation: Prioritizing organic growth (Durg, NE, Kutch); NECEM acquisition liabilities settled (INR12.5cr), remaining consideration (INR10cr non-compete + INR4cr equity) to close in Q1FY27; Dividend policy not discussed.
risks & watch-items: Sustained Middle East conflict driving fuel costs; Delay in Nagaur due to Supreme Court Aravalli ruling; Pricing power inability to pass through INR400/ton cost hike; Clinker availability constraint (93% util) mitigated by blended ratio improvement (62% -> 65%+).
management quality / tone: Cautiously optimistic on volume (>industry growth) but transparent on margin compression; Confident on long-term 30MT goal despite Assam mining setback; Defensive on cost mitigation levers.
non-obvious takeaways: Derecognition of INR325cr intangible assets (mining rights) due to AMDCL contract cancellation in Assam, yet management confirms viability of NE plant via 2 alternative auctioned mines (250MT reserves); RMC growth deliberately curbed to focus on higher-margin non-cement products like adhesives.

themes.title: Cement demand & pricing recovery
themes.need: Q1FY27 turned cement from a pricing story into a volume-share-plus-fuel-cost story. ULTRACEMCO grew domestic grey volume +13.1% YoY against an estimated ~7-8% industry, delivered its first Rs 5,000cr+ April-June EBITDA (Rs 5,146cr) with EBITDA/ton held above Rs 1,200, and crossed 200.1 MT domestic capacity a year early - but guided Q2FY27 cost UP ~Rs 130-140/ton and pinned the Rs 1,400/ton consolidated target to Q4FY28. The fuel shock, not price, is the swing factor: JKCEMENT's EBITDA/ton fell to Rs 982 from Rs 1,229 YoY despite +19% grey volume, DALBHARAT flagged pet coke 'surged to nearly $160/t' versus a pre-war $110-115, and NUVOCO defended INR 1,079/ton EBITDA only by cutting petcoke from 37% to 27% of fuel mix in a single quarter. Consolidation is visibly compounding (INDIACEM EBITDA/ton Rs 386->400->509->603 across four quarters; DALBHARAT closed Jaypee at Rs 2,850cr EV with Chunar operational and Rewa on trial within 50 days) even as DALBHARAT slipped its 75mt milestone from FY27 to FY28. SHREECEM/RAMCOCEM/JKLAKSHMI/JSWCEMENT/STARCEMENT/BIRLACORPN ride the same volume + consolidation axis.
themes.driver: Q2FY27 is the guided cost trough - ULTRACEMCO ~Rs 130-140/ton, JKCEMENT ~Rs 150/ton and BIRLACORPN Rs 70-80/ton of incremental cost; then fuel-mix agility (NUVOCO's petcoke swing) and whether DALBHARAT's ~Rs 150/t of procurement savings is really 'permanent, not timing'.

business_model.body: JK Lakshmi Cement Ltd. manufactures and sells cement and clinker (91% of turnover, NIC code 2394), operating 3 integrated cement plants and 4 grinding units across India. demand_drivers.body:
- Indian cement demand grew ~7% in FY2025-26, driven by government-led infrastructure programmes (PM Gati Shakti, Bharatmala, Smart Cities Mission, PMAY) and rising urbanisation/housing demand in rural and semi-urban markets.
- Industry volumes are projected to expand at 6-7% per annum in the medium term, and demand is projected to grow 6-7% in FY2026-27, driven by housing and infrastructure, roads, railways, affordable housing, and Tier-II city development.
- Cement price realisations remained under pressure throughout FY2025-26 due to regional competitive dynamics and continued capacity additions, and are expected to stay range-bound near term.
- The West Asia conflict in Q4 FY2025-26 introduced a fresh cost headwind — pet coke, LNG, diesel and freight costs, plus rupee depreciation — compressing industry and Company margins with limited ability to pass through costs in a competitive pricing environment.
- Ongoing consolidation among top industry players is expected to support pricing discipline over time, though industry capacity utilisation is projected to stay around ~70% even on an expanded base in FY2026-27.
- Domestic coal substitution (reducing Hormuz-linked import exposure) is viewed as a lever that, if sustained, structurally improves cost stability.
- The shared industry cost shock is seen as providing a rare justification for cement price hikes being passed on to consumers.
- Company outperformed the industry (10% volume growth vs ~7% industry growth) on the strength of market presence, distribution network depth, and customer trust; total capacity reached 18 million tonnes with the Surat Grinding Unit addition.
- Regional demand variation: Central and Northern regions led volume growth, Western and Eastern markets followed closely, while the South saw minimal volume growth.
- Management is prioritising profitable volume growth, Smart Building Solutions and premium products, and deeper regional market presence to navigate range-bound pricing and cost headwinds into FY2026-27.

margins.title: Margins & cost dynamics
margins.body: Fuel cost surge: Petcoke +40% QoQ (~$160/ton), Coal +30% QoQ; Guided cost increase INR300/ton (energy) + INR80-100/ton (packaging); Mitigation via fuel mix change in North, renewable energy (46% mix), AI/ML in pyro/grinding.

capital_allocation.title: Capital allocation
capital_allocation.body: Prioritizing organic growth (Durg, NE, Kutch); NECEM acquisition liabilities settled (INR12.5cr), remaining consideration (INR10cr non-compete + INR4cr equity) to close in Q1FY27; Dividend policy not discussed.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: During FY2025-26, JKLC commissioned an additional Grinding Unit of 1.35 million tonnes at Surat and completed de-bottlenecking of its Cement Mill at Sirohi, taking total Company cement capacity to 18 MnMT. In June 2025, JK Lakshmi Cement Ltd. and Udaipur Cement Works Ltd. completed a landmark merger, strengthening scale, synergies and sustainability commitment, expanding geographic presence and reinforcing financial resilience. Renewable capacity additions during the year included a 9 MW solar plant at Phalodi, a 2.75 MW Floating Solar Power Plant at the Udaipur Integrated Unit, and a 7 MW solar plant at JKLC, taking total Solar Power Capacity to 124 MW from 112.10 MW. On the Smart Building Solutions (SBS) front, 5 new RMC plants were commissioned across Bhopal, Faridabad, Bhavnagar, Indore, and Durg; Tile Adhesive production was launched; and two additional Gypsum Plaster trading units were added in Rajasthan. The Company's limestone mine acquisition in Assam continues to underpin its long-term strategic commitment to the high-growth Eastern market. Separately, several projects are in the environmental-clearance pipeline per FY2025-26 EIA disclosures: expansion of limestone production capacity at the Durg (Chhattisgarh) Mine Lease II from 0.3 to 1.35 Million TPA; expansion of the captive limestone mines at Mine Lease I (Durg) from 4.8 to 8 Million TPA; a proposed standalone Cement Grinding Project of 3.0 Million TPA at Lohat, Madhubani (Bihar) for OPC/PSC/PPC/Composite Cement; and a proposed new limestone mine 'Mudhvay Sub Block A' with 2.5 Million TPA capacity at Kachchh, Gujarat. An Integrated Cement Plant proposal (Clinker 0.95 Million TPA, Cement 0.95 Million TPA producing OPC/PPC/PSC/Composite Cement) is also referenced in the EIA disclosures, though the source text is truncated before further project detail.

management_tone.title: Management quality / tone
management_tone.body: Cautiously optimistic on volume (>industry growth) but transparent on margin compression; Confident on long-term 30MT goal despite Assam mining setback; Defensive on cost mitigation levers.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Part of the JK Organisation, a diversified industrial group with a 140+ year legacy, lending brand trust and institutional depth
- Renewable power meets ~47% of total electrical consumption, among the best ratios in the industry, supporting cost and ESG positioning
- Nationally distributed operational footprint (3 integrated plants + 4 grinding units across 20 states) enabling efficient market access and logistics optimisation
- June 2025 merger with Udaipur Cement Works Ltd. strengthened scale, synergies, and financial resilience
- Digitalisation push (AI/ML/IoT, RPA, AI-based Advanced Process Control at Udaipur) improving efficiency and cost control
- Long-term credit rating of AA (Stable) from CRISIL and CARE, and highest short-term rating A1+ from both, supporting access to capital
- Limestone mine acquisition in Assam underpins long-term strategic commitment to the high-growth Eastern market
- Low-carbon product innovation (Green PRO LC3) launched at Sirohi, differentiating on sustainability

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body: Sustained Middle East conflict driving fuel costs; Delay in Nagaur due to Supreme Court Aravalli ruling; Pricing power inability to pass through INR400/ton cost hike; Clinker availability constraint (93% util) mitigated by blended ratio improvement (62% -> 65%+).

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body: Derecognition of INR325cr intangible assets (mining rights) due to AMDCL contract cancellation in Assam, yet management confirms viability of NE plant via 2 alternative auctioned mines (250MT reserves); RMC growth deliberately curbed to focus on higher-margin non-cement products like adhesives.

strategy.title: Strategies (RHP)
strategy.body:
- Three strategic priorities for FY2025-26 and beyond: capacity expansion, cost leadership, and sustainability.
- Capacity expansion programme toward 30 million tonnes by 2030, via a phased roadmap of greenfield and brownfield investments.
- Efficiency enhancement programme delivering cost savings across plant operations, logistics, discount rationalisation, and geo-mix optimisation to provide structural cost insulation.
- Prioritising profitable volume growth, advancing Smart Building Solutions (SBS) and premium product portfolio, deepening ESG leadership, and reinforcing presence in high-potential …

other.title: Notable from the deck
other.body:
- [Promoter structure] The Company states it has only one Promoter, namely Bengal & Assam Company Limited, and that Dwarkesh Energy Limited is a Promoter Group entity and not a Promoter as IiAS had reported; Smt. Vinita Singhania is described as a constituent of the Promoter Group and not the Promoter.
- [AGM / Governance] IiAS recommended AGAINST Item 5 of the AGM Notice — re-appointment of Smt. Vinita Singhania as Chairperson & Managing Director for five years from 01 August 2026 with remuneration fixed as minimum remuneration — citing (G) Governance Concern and (T) Weak Transparency; the Company asked IiAS to change the recommendation from AGAINST to FOR and issue an Addendum.
- [Remuneration framework] The Company states the total remuneration (Fixed and Variable) of Smt. Vinita Singhania together with the Dy. Managing Director (Shri Shrivats Singhania) and President & Director (Dr. Arun Kumar Shukla) shall be within the permitted limit of 10% of Net Profit for all managerial personnel under Section 197 of the Companies Act, 2013, with minimum remuneration and no commission in the event of loss or inadequate profits under Section IV of Part II of Schedule V.
- [Variable pay] The Company declines to quantify a cap: it states that since it is difficult to project future profits, neither the Commission nor an absolute cap on variable pay can be quantified at this stage, and that the Performance Linked Incentive is only an enabling approval as the Company presently does not have any PLI Scheme.
- [NRC process] The Company states Smt. Vinita Singhania abstained when her remuneration and re-appointment were discussed in the Nomination & Remuneration Committee (chaired by an Independent Director) and that the matter was approved by all the Independent Directors forming part of the NRC, hence no conflict of interest.
